correctness.rationale: The exact support formula identifies the Euclidean width of a root polytope with twice the maximum of signed Gaussian edge differences after independent chi normalization. The hub-leaf block tends in \(L^2\), after Gaussian-maximal centering, to \(|Z|\); the disjoint internal-handle block is one-dependent and has a Gumbel extremal law by a signed adjacent-tail estimate plus local-dependence Poisson approximation. Its coarse deviations vanish in \(L^2\). The inverse-chi fourth moment estimate shows the spherical correction is \(o_{L^2}(1)\) and \(o_{\Pr}(s_p)\), the latter being the Gumbel scale. A three-way maximum of the two blocks and the tight bridge yields the claimed trichotomy, critical atom and exposure shares. Normal-density integration gives the first two critical moments. VERIFY.py confirms finite exact support/covariance identities and numerical diagnostics but is not used as proof of the infinite conclusions.

originality.rationale: The theorem derives a new sharp broom-width distribution trichotomy with a critical atom and exposed-edge phase split. The older root-polytope result giving the leading mean-width limit set for all trees including brooms does not imply the second-order fluctuation distribution or conditional edge selection. Existing regular-matroid/crosspolytope and facet statements are structural, while classical 1-dependent Gaussian maxima alone do not identify the geometric hub/path competition, its stretched-exponential parameter window, atom, or width variance. value.rationale: All tree symmetric-edge polytopes are crosspolytopes with identical dimension, face lattice and Euclidean volume for fixed order; Euclidean random widths can nevertheless show different limiting laws. The natural broom simultaneously carries highly dependent hub leaves and a one-dependent Gaussian handle. Their competition at \(h\) on the scale \(p^2\exp(\lambda\sqrt{\log p})\) yields a sharp limiting atom and exposed-vertex-family phase diagram, as well as explicit critical variance. This motivated second-order geometric invariant is not a small parameter tweak of the already-known first-order all-tree mean-width range and could guide the analysis of other graphs with competing Gaussian extreme structures.
